title: PerQ: Inverse Generative Modeling for Neural Image Compression via Quantization Error Compensation

paper.title: PerQ: Inverse Generative Modeling for Neural Image Compression via Quantization Error Compensation
paper.abstract: Abstract Neural image codecs face a fundamental trade-off between pixel fidelity and perceptual quality. Distortion-optimized codecs preserve pixel-wise fidelity but produce blurred reconstructions at low bitrates, whereas generative codecs leverage learned priors to improve perceptual quality but tend to exhibit saturating PSNR at higher bitrates and require separate models for different bitrate targets. We propose PerQ , which reframes perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling with bounded support. Specifically, we define the quantization cell as the set of latents that yield the same transmitted symbols and derive a transport bound showing that reconstructions from this cell remain within a rate-determined radius of the codec output. This motivates performing generative reconstruction within the codec-induced quantization cell, rather than sampling from an unconstrained image prior. PerQ implements this principle by attaching a rate-conditioned flow-matching compensator to a frozen, multi-rate distortion-optimized backbone, enabling perceptual enhancement while preserving the backbone’s coding performance. Experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020 show that PerQ achieves perceptual performance comparable to generative codecs such as MS-ILLM in LPIPS and FID, while maintaining competitive PSNR relative to distortion-optimized codecs such as ELIC. A single model checkpoint supports a wide bitrate range with fast decoding, and the compensator provides consistent gains across three different backbones. The implementation is available at https://jasminepp.github.io/PerQ/ .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image compression has long been a fundamental research topic in signal processing and a core component of modern visual data infrastructure Bull and Zhang (2021) . Conventional image codecs such as JPEG Wallace (1991) , BPG Bellard (2018) , and the intra modes of AV1 Han et al. (2021) and VVC Bross et al. (2021) , have been widely adopted over the past decades. More recently, end-to-end learned image compression Ballé et al. (2017) ; Ballé et al. (2018) ; Minnen and Singh (2020) have achieved competitive or superior rate-distortion performance compared with conventional codecs based on pixel-wise metrics, such as PSNR Wang and Bovik (2009) . However, optimizing pixel-wise distortion does not necessarily yield perceptually pleasing reconstructions, especially at low bitrates, where severe bitrate constraints limit the preservation of fine details and high-frequency image content, often resulting in visually blurred reconstructions. This limitation has motivated growing interest in perceptual image compression, which prioritizes perceptual fidelity over pixel-wise similarity and has led to the development of perceptual and generative image codecs. Recent generative codecs have demonstrated promising perceptual quality at extremely low bitrates Jia et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026) . However, extending this perceptual advantage to practical deployment remains challenging. (i) Pixel-wise fidelity : downstream applications often require reconstructions to remain faithful to the source pixels, but most generative codecs, whose reconstructions are dominated by a generative prior, tend to plateau on PSNR even as the bitrate becomes high, since additional bits do not bring the prior closer to the source pixels Mentzer et al. (2020) ; Muckley et al. (2023) . (ii) Bitrate coverage : practical deployment would benefit from a single model that supports a broad range of bitrates, avoiding the need to store and maintain separate models for different rates. However, most existing perceptual codecs require separate models for different target rates Mentzer et al. (2020) ; Zhang et al. (2025) . Although a few approaches support multiple bitrates with a single model Careil et al. (2024) ; Guo et al. (2025) , their operating ranges are typically concentrated in a relatively narrow low-bitrate window. The results of existing works shown in Table 1 reveal that none of them delivers high perceptual quality, competitive pixel fidelity, and wide bitrate coverage with a single trained model. Figure 1 : Balance between Perceptual quality and pixel fidelity. (Left) Visual comparison at comparable bitrates, with PSNR (dB) / LPIPS. (Right) BD-rate of PSNR against BD-rate of LPIPS on CLIC2020-test, both relative to VTM intra, lower is better). We ask, Can these competing objectives be reconciled within a single codec without sacrificing the advantages of distortion-optimized compression? We propose PerQ , an image codec that reframes perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling with bounded support , leveraging the quantization structure of an existing codec to constrain perceptual refinement. We characterize the set of latent representations that yield the same transmitted symbols as a quantization cell and derive a transport bound relating the quantization step to a rate-determined radius in pixel space. Unlike prior approaches that augment distortion-optimized backbones with perceptual losses He et al. (2022b) ; Körber et al. (2024) ; Mentzer et al. (2020) and use learned generative priors to explore the image manifold, PerQ employs a flow-matching-based compensator as a decoder-side plug-in to improve perceptual quality while keeping the refined latent within this bounded region. Integrated into the decoder, the compensator leaves the bitstream unchanged and supports the backbone’s existing multi-rate operating range with a single model, while retaining fast decoding. Importantly, the derived transport bound guarantees that the refined reconstruction remains within a rate-determined pixel-space radius of the backbone’s output, even with perceptual optimization. This design brings together the perceptual advantages of generative codecs, the pixel fidelity of distortion-optimized codecs, and broad bitrate coverage within a single model ( Figure 1 ). The main contributions of this work are: • (C1) Inverse generative modeling with bounded support. We formulate perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling over a rate-determined bounded support, characterized by a transport bound (§ 3.1 ) that relates the quantization step to a pixel-space radius around the output of a multi-rate distortion-optimized codec. • (C2) A rate-conditioned flow-matching compensator design is designed (§ 3.3 ) for perceptual reconstruction within the bounded support. A single checkpoint supports multiple backbone rates, while the decoder-side design preserves the bitstream and generalizes across different backbones. • (C3) PerQ: A perceptual-fidelity-balanced image codec integrates a bounded-support compensator with a frozen distortion-optimized backbone, bridging the gap between generative perceptual codecs and distortion-oriented codecs by combining strong perceptual quality with competitive pixel fidelity in a single, multi-rate model. Extensive experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020-test ( Table 1 ) show that PerQ retains most of the perceptual gains of strong generative codecs such as MS-ILLM while achieving competitive pixel fidelity against VVC (VTM intra), while enabling efficient four-step decoding at 86 86 ms/MP. Moreover, a single checkpoint covers nearly two orders of magnitude in bitrate, and the same compensator delivers consistent gains across two additional backbones. These results demonstrate that PerQ balances perceptual quality, pixel fidelity, and bitrate flexibility within a single, efficient codec. sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Learned image compression originates from the joint optimization of an analysis/synthesis transform and a learned entropy model Theis et al. (2017) ; Ballé et al. (2017) , with subsequent progress driven primarily by more effective entropy models and stronger transforms. Hyperpriors capture spatially-varying scale Ballé et al. (2018) ; discretized Gaussian mixture likelihoods refine the conditional entropy model Cheng et al. (2020) ; channel-wise autoregressive factorizations sharpen it further Minnen and Singh (2020) ; checkerboard contexts parallelize spatial autoregression He et al. (2021) ; and recent designs combine grouped channel attention He et al. (2022a) with multi-reference context Jiang et al. (2023) ; Jiang et al. (2025) or transformer-CNN hybrid transforms Liu et al. (2023a) . The best performing neural image codecs match or exceed VVC all intra mode on both PSNR and MS-SSIM, with real-time variants closing the latency gap Jia et al. (2025) , and they remain visually faithful across moderate to high bitrates. The picture changes at low rates, where the bit budget is limited to preserve high-frequency content, and reconstructions become visibly blurred. The results in Blau and Michaeli (2018) ; Blau and Michaeli (2019) show that the divergence between source and reconstruction marginals widens at low rates and cannot be closed with further distortion-oriented training. Generative image codecs are designed to primarily target lower bitrates by conditioning reconstructions on a generative prior trained to match natural-image statistics, trading pixel-wise fidelity for perceptual realism. GAN-based codecs integrate adversarial training into the rate-distortion objective Tschannen et al. (2018) ; Agustsson et al. (2019) ; Mentzer et al. (2020) ; Muckley et al. (2023) ; He et al. (2022b) , with subsequent work exposing the distortion-perception trade-off during decoding Agustsson et al. (2023) ; Körber et al. (2024) and obtaining variable-rate operation from a single codec Li et al. (2025a) . Alternatively, diffusion-based codecs employ learned denoising at the decoder, with early work casting compression as reverse channel coding of noise samples through a Gaussian diffusion process Theis et al. (2022) . Follow-up studies generalize this to pretrained foundation priors Vonderfecht and Liu (2025) and perform multi-rate operations on top of a frozen prior Jia et al. (2026) . A separate line trains a conditional diffusion model as the codec decoder. CDC Yang and Mandt (2023) replaces the VAE decoder with a conditional diffusion model, PerCo Careil et al. (2024) couples a spatial latent with a global textual code for ultra-low-rate decoding, and other designs guide a frozen text-to-image or semantic prior Lei et al. (2023) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Relic et al. (2024) ; Hoogeboom et al. (2023) with compressed content. These designs typically incur multi-step sampling costs during decoding. More recent work distills the iterative process into a single step Jia et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) ; Guo et al. (2025) ; Xue et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2026) . Since reconstruction is conditioned on the generative prior rather than driven by the bitstream alone, pixel-space fidelity saturates as bpp increases, and PSNR improves sub-linearly with rate. Moreover, most designs commit to a single rate point at training time, requiring a separate model per operating point on the rate-distortion curve.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: As mentioned in Section 1 , unconstrained generative compression typically conditions reconstructions on a learned image prior, often incurring a penalty in pixel-wise fidelity as a result. This design is acceptable in applications that can tolerate hallucinated details and deviations from source fidelity, as opposed to distortion-oriented codecs. In this paper, we aim to close the perceptual gap of distortion-optimized image codecs while preserving reconstructions that remain faithful to the source. To this end, we constrain perceptual reconstruction within the quantization-error space induced by the compression backbone. In this section, we first derive the structural properties of this constraint in § 3.1 and § 3.2 . We then propose a flow-matching based compensator in § 3.3 , which is integrated with a compression codec backbone (§ 3.3.2 ). We describe the training methodology in § 3.4 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Bounded-support Modeling
sections.text: The transport bound turns the quantization cell from an error characterization into a feasible region for perceptual reconstruction. In the latent space, ( 3 ) defines the quantization cell 𝒞 ⁡ ( y ^ , q ) = { y ′ : ‖ y ′ − y ^ ‖ ∞ ≤ q / 2 } \mathcal{C}(\hat{y},q)=\{\,y^{\prime}:\|y^{\prime}-\hat{y}\|_{\infty}\leq q/2\,\} around the latent y ^ \hat{y} : the source latent y y lies in this cell, and every latent in it rounds to the same transmitted symbols. In the pixel space, ( 5 ) confines every reconstruction decoded from the cell to the closed ball ℬ ⁡ ( x ^ , q ) := { u : ‖ u − x ^ ‖ 2 ≤ R ⁡ ( q ) } \mathcal{B}(\hat{x},q):=\{\,u:\|u-\hat{x}\|_{2}\leq R(q)\,\} around the backbone reconstruction x ^ = f θ dec ​ ( y ^ ) \hat{x}=f^{\mathrm{dec}}_{\theta}(\hat{y}) . This ball constrains decoder outputs relative to x ^ \hat{x} , rather than bounding the reconstruction error relative to the source image x x , which also depends on the distortion introduced by the encoder-decoder transform. This transform-induced distortion remains fixed once the backbone is frozen (§ 3.3.2 ). The rate-distortion-perception trade-off Blau and Michaeli (2018) ; Blau and Michaeli (2019) implies that a distortion-optimized backbone may retain a perceptual distribution gap d p ​ ( p X , p X ^ ) > 0 d_{p}(p_{X},p_{\hat{X}})>0 . Rather than recovering the source latent itself, we formulate perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling over the quantization cell, treating it as a feasible design space in which to seek perceptually enhanced reconstructions. Accordingly, we introduce a compensator ψ \psi that models the conditional distribution: y ~ ∼ p ψ ​ ( y ~ ∣ y ^ , z ^ , q ) , supp ​ p ψ ⊆ 𝒞 ⁡ ( y ^ , q ) , \tilde{y}\sim p_{\psi}(\tilde{y}\mid\hat{y},\hat{z},q),\qquad\mathrm{supp}\,p_{\psi}\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\hat{y},q), (6) in which z ^ \hat{z} is the auxiliary latent produced by the backbone’s hyper-prior and the support is enforced by clamping at the decoder side (§ 3.3.1 ). Every sample y ~ \tilde{y} quantizes to the same transmitted symbols, and its decoded image lies within ℬ ⁡ ( x ^ , q ) \mathcal{B}(\hat{x},q) . Unlike prior work Yi et al. (2026) , which models quantization error as a latent-recovery problem by adding learned noise to y ^ \hat{y} to approximate the source latent y y , PerQ treats the quantization cell as a design space. Any y ~ \tilde{y} within the cell is a valid reconstruction candidate, and the goal is to find one whose decoded image better closes the perceptual gap, rather than to recover y y exactly. Moreover, as shown in Appendix A , matching the conditional distribution of the source latent would reproduce the distribution of the unquantized reconstruction.

To keep the velocity field at one operating scale across rate points, we multiply the flow state r t r_{t} by q q before the network, and divide the output by q q to return to symbol space, where the bound of ( 10 ) is applied. We observe that this scaling improves performance over operating directly in symbol space. The hyper-prior latent z ^ \hat{z} is upsampled by 4 × 4{\times} to the spatial resolution of y ^ \hat{y} through two stages of 3 × 3 3{\times}3 convolution and 2 × 2{\times} pixel shuffle with a SiLU activation in between. sections.heading: 3.3.2 Compression backbone
sections.text: We focus on modeling the quantization-error space and adopt an existing neural image compression model as the codec backbone with minor modifications. Specifically, we use the intra-frame model of DCVC-RT Jia et al. (2025) , which delivers strong rate–distortion performance at low complexity, supports fast encoding and decoding, and provides variable-bitrate coding by selecting a quantization parameter for the target rate point. One implementation detail of Jia et al. (2025) is that the quantization step size is applied at two stages on both the encoder and decoder sides. The encoder f ϕ enc f^{\mathrm{enc}}_{\phi} is decomposed into two sub-networks f ϕ enc1 f^{\mathrm{enc}1}_{\phi} and f ϕ enc2 f^{\mathrm{enc}2}_{\phi} : the rate-specific parameter q enc q^{\mathrm{enc}} is applied between them, and the per-pixel parameter q local enc q^{\mathrm{enc}}_{\mathrm{local}} (predicted by the hyper-prior) is applied at the bottleneck: y sym = f ϕ enc2 ​ ( ( f ϕ enc1 ​ ( x ) ⋅ q enc ) ⋅ q local enc CLOSE . y^{\mathrm{sym}}=f^{\mathrm{enc}2}_{\phi}\bigl((f^{\mathrm{enc}1}_{\phi}(x)\cdot q^{\mathrm{enc}}\bigr)\cdot q^{\mathrm{enc}}_{\mathrm{local}}. sections.heading: 3.4 Training
sections.text: Stage 1: Backbone training. We first train the variable-rate compression backbone with the rate-distortion objective R + λ ​ D R+\lambda D , following the typical image compression training pipeline Ballé et al. (2018) . We then freeze the encoder, decoder, and entropy models, preserving the quantization structure of ( 3 ) exactly. Stage 2: Compensator training. We train the compensator with a combined objective comprising the rectified-flow loss ( 9 ), distortion and perceptual terms, and an adversarial term: ℒ = λ ⁡ ( ℒ MSE + ℒ E-LPIPS ) + λ FM ​ ℒ FM + λ GAN ​ ℒ GAN , \mathcal{L}=\lambda\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{E-LPIPS}}\bigr)+\lambda_{\text{FM}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}+\lambda_{\text{GAN}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}, (15) where ℒ E-LPIPS \mathcal{L}_{\text{E-LPIPS}} is the E-LPIPS perceptual distance Zhang et al. (2018) ; Kettunen et al. (2019) , ℒ F ​ M \mathcal{L}_{FM} is the flow matching loss Liu et al. (2023b) , and ℒ GAN \mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}} is a generator loss against a patch discriminator conditioned on the rate point (cf. Mentzer et al. (2020) ; Yi et al. (2026) ). sections.heading: 4 Experimental Configurations
sections.text: Implementation Details. We use the intra-frame model of DCVC-RT Jia et al. (2025) as our default compression backbone, supporting 64 rate points, with the architectural modifications described in Section 3.3.2 . We trained it from scratch on the MLIC training dataset Jiang et al. (2023) ; Jiang et al. (2025) , with a batch size of 64 for 1M steps in the first stage (backbone training) and a batch size of 16 for 200K steps in the second stage (compensator training). More training details and configurations are provided in the Appendix B . Evaluation. We evaluate PerQ on Kodak Eastman Kodak Company () (24 images at 768 × 512 768\times 512 ), CLIC2020-test CLIC (2020) (428 images at ∼ \sim 2K resolution). We measure pixel fidelity using PSNR in RGB space, and perceptual quality using LPIPS Zhang et al. (2018) , DISTS Ding et al. (2022) , and FID Heusel et al. (2017) computed on 256 × 256 256{\times}256 patches following Muckley et al. (2023) . Benchmark Methods. We compare against four baseline categories. The conventional reference is VVC (VTM-22.0 intra) Bross et al. (2021) . For distortion-optimal learned codecs we include ELIC He et al. (2022a) (PSNR anchor), EVC Wang et al. (2023) and DCVC-RT intra Jia et al. (2025) . For GAN-based generative codecs we include MS-ILLM Muckley et al. (2023) (perceptual anchor), HiFiC Mentzer et al. (2020) , and Control-GIC Li et al. (2025a) . For diffusion-based generative codecs, we include PerCo Careil et al. (2024) , CDC Yang and Mandt (2023) , DiffEIC Li et al. (2025b) , StableCodec Zhang et al. (2025) , and OSCAR Guo et al. (2025) . All neural baselines are re-run from publicly available checkpoints. Reconstructions are generated on a single NVIDIA-4090 GPU, except for DiffEIC Li et al. (2025b) , whose 50-step decoding is prohibitively slow on the 4090 and is therefore generated on NVIDIA-H200. Decoding latency and complexity reported in Table 1 are measured on a single NVIDIA-4090 GPU for fair comparison.

sections.text: Quantitative comparison. Table 1 and Figure 4 position PerQ across the deployment Pareto frontier on the Kodak and CLIC2020-test datasets. With a single checkpoint, PerQ performs close to ELIC on PSNR ( − 1.6 % -1.6\% vs. − 2.0 % -2.0\% BD-rate against VVC on Kodak, + 2.7 % +2.7\% vs. − 1.9 % -1.9\% on CLIC2020-test) while achieving large perceptual gains ( − 57.4 % -57.4\% in LPIPS, − 63.2 % -63.2\% in DISTS and − 67.9 % -67.9\% in FID on Kodak, and − 70.6 % -70.6\% , − 77.4 % -77.4\% and − 91.9 % -91.9\% on CLIC2020-test). As shown in Figure 1 (right), PerQ is the only codec that combines such perceptual gains with VVC-level PSNR, whereas existing perceptual codecs offer significantly inferior PSNR performance ( + 89.9 % +89.9\% BD-rate against VVC for MS-ILLM and + 116.3 % +116.3\% for HiFiC on CLIC2020-test). It can also be observed that per-rate trained generative codecs achieve higher perceptual BD-rate gains (e.g., MS-ILLM, StableCodec), but they require separate checkpoints per rate point or operate over narrower rate ranges. Qualitative comparison. Figure 1 (left) and Figure 5 compare reconstructions at comparable bitrates. At low rates, ELIC produces visibly blurred textures, while generative codecs recover sharpness but with a substantial PSNR drop (more than 5 5 dB below ELIC). PerQ recovers much of this sharpness with PSNR results close to ELIC. In Figure 1 , for example, it matches the LPIPS of OSCAR with a 6.5 6.5 dB higher PSNR. At high rates, generative codecs introduce unfaithful texture details, while PerQ delivers sharpness with similarly high fidelity to ELIC ( 28.22 28.22 vs. 28.40 28.40 dB) using the fewest bits. This pattern confirms the quantitative results in Table 1 and verifies the effectiveness of the bounded compensator. More visual examples are available in Appendix D . Ablation Study. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented PerQ, a learning-based image codec that addresses the trade-off between pixel-wise fidelity and perceptual quality by formulating perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling with bounded support. Specifically, we characterized the quantization cell of a multi-rate distortion-optimized codec as the set of latents that yield the same transmitted symbols, and derived a transport bound that constrains the deviation of reconstructions within this cell from the backbone’s output. Building on this formulation, we developed a rate-conditioned flow-matching compensator that performs perceptual reconstruction within the codec-induced bounded support, preserving the backbone’s multi-rate capability. Experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020-test demonstrate that PerQ achieves strong perceptual quality with competitive pixel fidelity, while supporting a wide bitrate range through a single model and efficient decoding. To the best of our knowledge, PerQ is the first generative image codec to combine these properties in a single framework.

sections.heading: Stage 1: backbone (distortion only).
sections.text: The compression backbone (DCVC-RT intra-frame model [ 25 ] ) is trained from scratch on the MLIC training set [ 29 , 28 ] with the rate-distortion objective L = R + λ ⋅ L MSE L=R+\lambda\cdot L_{\text{MSE}} for 1M steps at batch size 64. The Lagrange multiplier λ \lambda is sampled from [4, 4096] for 64 rate points, following [ 35 ] . We use the AdamW optimizer [ 41 ] with ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999) and weight decay 10 − 2 10^{-2} . The peak learning rate is 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , reached by a linear warmup from 10 − 6 10^{-6} over the first 100K steps, with a multi-step schedule that halves the learning rate at 50 % 50\% , 75 % 75\% , 87.5 % 87.5\% , and 93.75 % 93.75\% of training. Gradients are clipped to a global ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm of 1.0. Over the first 10 % 10\% of training, the weight of the rate term and λ \lambda are ramped up linearly, from 0 to 1 and from 4 to the sampled value, respectively. Training images are randomly cropped to 256 × 256 256{\times}256 .

sections.heading: Stage 2: compensator (perceptual optimization).
sections.text: In stage 2 we freeze the encoder, decoder, hyper-prior, and entropy models, and add the compensator and discriminator for joint training. We train for 200K steps at batch size 16 with λ ∈ [ 4 , 4096 ] \lambda\in[4,4096] and the Stage 2 objective of Section 3.4 . The weight of the latent flow-matching term is λ FM = 10 4 \lambda_{\text{FM}}=10^{4} , the weight of the adversarial term is λ GAN = 0.1 \lambda_{\text{GAN}}=0.1 , and the E-LPIPS term has the same weight as the MSE term. L E-LPIPS L_{\text{E-LPIPS}} uses the VGG backbone [ 30 , 61 , 49 ] during training; we report the LPIPS variant with AlexNet [ 32 ] features for evaluation. Optimizer and schedule follow stage 1, except the peak learning rate is 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , the warmup is 10K steps without the rate and λ \lambda warmup, and we keep the weight decay to 10 − 2 10^{-2} on the compensator’s and discriminator’s parameters. The GAN term is disabled for the first 20K iterations and then linearly warmed up over the next 20K iterations to its full weight.

sections.heading: Compensator architecture.
sections.text: The velocity field v ψ v_{\psi} is a stack of 10 ConvNeXt blocks [ 40 ] with hidden width of 512, an MLP expansion ratio of 4 and a kernel size of 5. It first computes the sum of a 1 × 1 1{\times}1 convolution of the scaled flow state q ​ r t q\,r_{t} and a 1 × 1 1{\times}1 convolution of the channel-wise concatenation of y ^ \hat{y} , the upsampled z ^ \hat{z} , and q q . Timestep conditioning is injected through a sinusoidal positional embedding followed by a linear layer with SiLU, and each block maps it through a zero-initialized linear layer to the shift, scale, and gate of an adaLN-zero modulation [ 47 ] . The output head is a LayerNorm followed by a zero-initialized 1 × 1 1{\times}1 convolution, which makes the compensator output only the bounded prior noise at the start of training, i.e., it acts as the identity up to this noise. We use 4 Euler steps for flow matching at both training and inference, with bound scale m = 0.1 m{=}0.1 (Eq. 10 ) and prior noise standard deviation σ = 0.029 ≈ m / 12 \sigma=0.029\approx m/\sqrt{12} (Section 3.3.1 ). The default compensator has 31.0M parameters. The compensator-size ablation ( v4.1 and v4.2 in Table 2 ) uses two smaller compensators that change only the hidden width and keep the depth, kernel size, bound and training recipe: PerQ- 0.5 × 0.5\times with a hidden width of 384 (18.1M parameters) and PerQ- 0.25 × 0.25\times with a hidden width of 256 (8.8M parameters).

sections.heading: Discriminator.
sections.text: The adversarial term uses a multi-scale rate-point-conditioned patch discriminator [ 43 ] with 3 spatial scales (input downsampled by 1 × , 2 × , 4 × 1{\times},2{\times},4{\times} via average pooling) and a separate per-rate-point parameterization (per-rate kernels at each conv layer). Each scale uses 3 strided convolutional layers with base width 48, doubled at each layer (capped at 512), followed by a 4 × 4 4{\times}4 stride-1 conv and a final 4 × 4 4{\times}4 patch logit head. All convolutions except the final logit head use spectral normalization [ 45 ] and LeakyReLU( 0.2 0.2 ) activations. The discriminator is trained jointly with the compensator, where both are updated at every step by the same AdamW optimizer, with hinge losses for the discriminator and the generator.

sections.heading: Backbones of the generality study.
sections.text: The three backbones of Table 4 are all trained from scratch on the MLIC training set with the Stage 1 objective, 64 rate points and the consolidated bottleneck quantization of Section 3.3.2 . DCVC-RT is the default backbone described above. ELIC [ 20 ] keeps its original architecture (320 latent channels in five uneven groups) and follows the DCVC-RT recipe, except that λ \lambda is sampled from [ 32 , 4096 ] [32,4096] . MLIC++ [ 28 ] keeps its original architecture (320 latent channels in 10 slices) with λ ∈ [ 32 , 4096 ] \lambda\in[32,4096] . It is first trained for 1M steps on 256 × 256 256{\times}256 crops at batch size 64 with a peak learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and then fine-tuned for 400K steps on 512 × 512 512{\times}512 crops at batch size 32, with a peak learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , 5K warmup steps, no rate or λ \lambda warmup, and the learning rate halved at 37.5 % 37.5\% , 75 % 75\% , 87.5 % 87.5\% , and 93.75 % 93.75\% of the fine-tuning. Since λ ≥ 32 \lambda\geq 32 , ELIC and MLIC++ do not reach the lowest rates of DCVC-RT (see the bpp ranges in Table 4 ). On each backbone, the compensator and all Stage 2 settings are those of the default model, except that λ \lambda follows the range of the backbone and MLIC++ is trained on 512 × 512 512{\times}512 crops.

sections.heading: Appendix D More visual results
sections.text: Figures 7 , 8 , and 9 compares the visual quality of the backbone models (DCVC-RT [ 25 ] and MLIC++ [ 28 ] ) with PerQ. In all examples, PerQ significantly improve the visual quality, like synthesizing the texture which are missing in the original backbone outputs, and improving the the sharpness of the images. Additional visual comparison results for comparing with baseline methods are provided in Figures 10 , 11 . 10 provides more examples for the comparison with the frozen backbone and other generative-based codecs. In all of them, the compensator reduces LPIPS by 53 53 – 68 % 68\% (e.g., 0.279 → 0.088 0.279\rightarrow 0.088 for the lamp) at a cost of only 0.6 0.6 – 0.9 0.9 dB in PSNR. sections.text: Limitations. Alongside the positive characteristics, limitations still remain with PerQ. First, it does not reach the highest perceptual quality attained by fully generative codecs, although it remains very competitive on distortion-based metrics and has achieved a better trade-off between fidelity and realism. Moreover, our design relies on a frozen distortion-optimized backbone and jointly fine-tuning the backbone may further improve performance. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.27374v1 [cs.CV] 19 Oct 2026 PerQ: Inverse Generative Modeling for Neural Image Compression via Quantization Error Compensation Tianhao Peng Affiliation: Visual Information Lab, University of Bristol, UK Email: tianhao.peng@bristol.ac.uk Ho Man Kwan Affiliation: Visual Information Lab, University of Bristol, UK Email: hm.kwan@bristol.ac.uk Fan Zhang Affiliation: Visual Information Lab, University of Bristol, UK Email: fan.zhang@bristol.ac.uk Shan Liu Affiliation: Tencent Media Lab, Palo Alto, USA Email: dave.bull@bristol.ac.uk Dave Bull Affiliation: Visual Information Lab, University of Bristol, UK Email: shanl@global.tencent.com Abstract Neural image codecs face a fundamental trade-off between pixel fidelity and perceptual quality. Distortion-optimized codecs preserve pixel-wise fidelity but produce blurred reconstructions at low bitrates, whereas generative codecs leverage learned priors to improve perceptual quality but tend to exhibit saturating PSNR at higher bitrates and require separate models for different bitrate targets. We propose PerQ , which reframes perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling with bounded support. Specifically, we define the quantization cell as the set of latents that yield the same transmitted symbols and derive a transport bound showing that reconstructions from this cell remain within a rate-determined radius of the codec output. This motivates performing generative reconstruction within the codec-induced quantization cell, rather than sampling from an unconstrained image prior. PerQ implements this principle by attaching a rate-conditioned flow-matching compensator to a frozen, multi-rate distortion-optimized backbone, enabling perceptual enhancement while preserving the backbone’s coding performance. Experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020 show that PerQ achieves perceptual performance comparable to generative codecs such as MS-ILLM in LPIPS and FID, while maintaining competitive PSNR relative to distortion-optimized codecs such as ELIC. A single model checkpoint supports a wide bitrate range with fast decoding, and the compensator provides consistent gains across three different backbones. The implementation is available at https://jasminepp.github.io/PerQ/ . 1 Introduction Image compression has long been a fundamental research topic in signal processing and a core component of modern visual data infrastructure Bull and Zhang (2021) . Conventional image codecs such as JPEG Wallace (1991) , BPG Bellard (2018) , and the intra modes of AV1 Han et al. (2021) and VVC Bross et al. (2021) , have been widely adopted over the past decades. More recently, end-to-end learned image compression Ballé et al. (2017) ; Ballé et al. (2018) ; Minnen and Singh (2020) have achieved competitive or superior rate-distortion performance compared with conventional codecs based on pixel-wise metrics, such as PSNR Wang and Bovik (2009) . However, optimizing pixel-wise distortion does not necessarily yield perceptually pleasing reconstructions, especially at low bitrates, where severe bitrate constraints limit the preservation of fine details and high-frequency image content, often resulting in visually blurred reconstructions. This limitation has motivated growing interest in perceptual image compression, which prioritizes perceptual fidelity over pixel-wise similarity and has led to the development of perceptual and generative image codecs. Recent generative codecs have demonstrated promising perceptual quality at extremely low bitrates Jia et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026) . However, extending this perceptual advantage to practical deployment remains challenging. (i) Pixel-wise fidelity : downstream applications often require reconstructions to remain faithful to the source pixels, but most generative codecs, whose reconstructions are dominated by a generative prior, tend to plateau on PSNR even as the bitrate becomes high, since additional bits do not bring the prior closer to the source pixels Mentzer et al. (2020) ; Muckley et al. (2023) . (ii) Bitrate coverage : practical deployment would benefit from a single model that supports a broad range of bitrates, avoiding the need to store and maintain separate models for different rates. However, most existing perceptual codecs require separate models for different target rates Mentzer et al. (2020) ; Zhang et al. (2025) . Although a few approaches support multiple bitrates with a single model Careil et al. (2024) ; Guo et al. (2025) , their operating ranges are typically concentrated in a relatively narrow low-bitrate window. The results of existing works shown in Table 1 reveal that none of them delivers high perceptual quality, competitive pixel fidelity, and wide bitrate coverage with a single trained model. Figure 1 : Balance between Perceptual quality and pixel fidelity. (Left) Visual comparison at comparable bitrates, with PSNR (dB) / LPIPS. (Right) BD-rate of PSNR against BD-rate of LPIPS on CLIC2020-test, both relative to VTM intra, lower is better). We ask, Can these competing objectives be reconciled within a single codec without sacrificing the advantages of distortion-optimized compression? We propose PerQ , an image codec that reframes perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling with bounded support , leveraging the quantization structure of an existing codec to constrain perceptual refinement. We characterize the set of latent representations that yield the same transmitted symbols as a quantization cell and derive a transport bound relating the quantization step to a rate-determined radius in pixel space. Unlike prior approaches that augment distortion-optimized backbones with perceptual losses He et al. (2022b) ; Körber et al. (2024) ; Mentzer et al. (2020) and use learned generative priors to explore the image manifold, PerQ employs a flow-matching-based compensator as a decoder-side plug-in to improve perceptual quality while keeping the refined latent within this bounded region. Integrated into the decoder, the compensator leaves the bitstream unchanged and supports the backbone’s existing multi-rate operating range with a single model, while retaining fast decoding. Importantly, the derived transport bound guarantees that the refined reconstruction remains within a rate-determined pixel-space radius of the backbone’s output, even with perceptual optimization. This design brings together the perceptual advantages of generative codecs, the pixel fidelity of distortion-optimized codecs, and broad bitrate coverage within a single model ( Figure 1 ). The main contributions of this work are: • (C1) Inverse generative modeling with bounded support. We formulate perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling over a rate-determined bounded support, characterized by a transport bound (§ 3.1 ) that relates the quantization step to a pixel-space radius around the output of a multi-rate distortion-optimized codec. • (C2) A rate-conditioned flow-matching compensator design is designed (§ 3.3 ) for perceptual reconstruction within the bounded support. A single checkpoint supports multiple backbone rates, while the decoder-side design preserves the bitstream and generalizes across different backbones. • (C3) PerQ: A perceptual-fidelity-balanced image codec integrates a bounded-support compensator with a frozen distortion-optimized backbone, bridging the gap between generative perceptual codecs and distortion-oriented codecs by combining strong perceptual quality with competitive pixel fidelity in a single, multi-rate model. Extensive experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020-test ( Table 1 ) show that PerQ retains most of the perceptual gains of strong generative codecs such as MS-ILLM while achieving competitive pixel fidelity against VVC (VTM intra), while enabling efficient four-step decoding at 86 86 ms/MP. Moreover, a single checkpoint covers nearly two orders of magnitude in bitrate, and the same compensator delivers consistent gains across two additional backbones. These results demonstrate that PerQ balances perceptual quality, pixel fidelity, and bitrate flexibility within a single, efficient codec. (2017) ; Ballé et al. (2017) , with subsequent progress driven primarily by more effective entropy models and stronger transforms. Hyperpriors capture spatially-varying scale Ballé et al. (2018) ; discretized Gaussian mixture likelihoods refine the conditional entropy model Cheng et al. (2020) ; channel-wise autoregressive factorizations sharpen it further Minnen and Singh (2020) ; checkerboard contexts parallelize spatial autoregression He et al. (2021) ; and recent designs combine grouped channel attention He et al. (2022a) with multi-reference context Jiang et al. (2023) ; Jiang et al. (2025) or transformer-CNN hybrid transforms Liu et al. (2023a) . The best performing neural image codecs match or exceed VVC all intra mode on both PSNR and MS-SSIM, with real-time variants closing the latency gap Jia et al. (2025) , and they remain visually faithful across moderate to high bitrates. The picture changes at low rates, where the bit budget is limited to preserve high-frequency content, and reconstructions become visibly blurred. The results in Blau and Michaeli (2018) ; Blau and Michaeli (2019) show that the divergence between source and reconstruction marginals widens at low rates and cannot be closed with further distortion-oriented training. Generative image codecs are designed to primarily target lower bitrates by conditioning reconstructions on a generative prior trained to match natural-image statistics, trading pixel-wise fidelity for perceptual realism. GAN-based codecs integrate adversarial training into the rate-distortion objective Tschannen et al. (2018) ; Agustsson et al. (2019) ; Mentzer et al. (2020) ; Muckley et al. (2023) ; He et al. (2022b) , with subsequent work exposing the distortion-perception trade-off during decoding Agustsson et al. (2023) ; Körber et al. (2024) and obtaining variable-rate operation from a single codec Li et al. (2025a) . Alternatively, diffusion-based codecs employ learned denoising at the decoder, with early work casting compression as reverse channel coding of noise samples through a Gaussian diffusion process Theis et al. (2022) . Follow-up studies generalize this to pretrained foundation priors Vonderfecht and Liu (2025) and perform multi-rate operations on top of a frozen prior Jia et al. (2026) . A separate line trains a conditional diffusion model as the codec decoder. CDC Yang and Mandt (2023) replaces the VAE decoder with a conditional diffusion model, PerCo Careil et al. (2024) couples a spatial latent with a global textual code for ultra-low-rate decoding, and other designs guide a frozen text-to-image or semantic prior Lei et al. (2023) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Relic et al. (2024) ; Hoogeboom et al. (2023) with compressed content. These designs typically incur multi-step sampling costs during decoding. More recent work distills the iterative process into a single step Jia et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) ; Guo et al. (2025) ; Xue et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2026) . Since reconstruction is conditioned on the generative prior rather than driven by the bitstream alone, pixel-space fidelity saturates as bpp increases, and PSNR improves sub-linearly with rate. Moreover, most designs commit to a single rate point at training time, requiring a separate model per operating point on the rate-distortion curve. 3 Method As mentioned in Section 1 , unconstrained generative compression typically conditions reconstructions on a learned image prior, often incurring a penalty in pixel-wise fidelity as a result. This design is acceptable in applications that can tolerate hallucinated details and deviations from source fidelity, as opposed to distortion-oriented codecs. In this paper, we aim to close the perceptual gap of distortion-optimized image codecs while preserving reconstructions that remain faithful to the source. To this end, we constrain perceptual reconstruction within the quantization-error space induced by the compression backbone. In this section, we first derive the structural properties of this constraint in § 3.1 and § 3.2 . We then propose a flow-matching based compensator in § 3.3 , which is integrated with a compression codec backbone (§ 3.3.2 ). We describe the training methodology in § 3.4 . 3.1 The Transport Bound Let x ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 x\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} denote the source image, f ϕ enc f^{\mathrm{enc}}_{\phi} the encoder, f θ dec f^{\mathrm{dec}}_{\theta} the decoder, and y = f ϕ enc ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ h × w × C y=f^{\mathrm{enc}}_{\phi}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times C} the latent. In the latent space, ( 3 ) defines the quantization cell 𝒞 ⁡ ( y ^ , q ) = { y ′ : ‖ y ′ − y ^ ‖ ∞ ≤ q / 2 } \mathcal{C}(\hat{y},q)=\{\,y^{\prime}:\|y^{\prime}-\hat{y}\|_{\infty}\leq q/2\,\} around the latent y ^ \hat{y} : the source latent y y lies in this cell, and every latent in it rounds to the same transmitted symbols. This transform-induced distortion remains fixed once the backbone is frozen (§ 3.3.2 ). (2026) , which models quantization error as a latent-recovery problem by adding learned noise to y ^ \hat{y} to approximate the source latent y y , PerQ treats the quantization cell as a design space. Any y ~ \tilde{y} within the cell is a valid reconstruction candidate, and the goal is to find one whose decoded image better closes the perceptual gap, rather than to recover y y exactly. Moreover, as shown in Appendix A , matching the conditional distribution of the source latent would reproduce the distribution of the unquantized reconstruction. 3.3 Overall framework Figure 2 : PerQ overview.
